old_title: 'Great coach, terrible streamer' - Erasmus gets thumbs-down for his weird watchalong
new_title: 'Great coach, terrible streamer' - Erasmus gets thumbs-down for his weird watchalong
old_text:
Watchwithrassie.com had been the surprise internet sensation of the week. Logging on a few hours before South Africa kicked off against Ireland on Saturday, one thing was immediately clear. When it came to rugby's latest scandal - "RassieGate 3.0" as Bryan Habana called it - this was not a place for balanced debate.
Rassie Erasmus's "match-fixing" rant, in the aftermath of the Springboks' defeat by France in Paris, had caused a depressingly familiar furore and earned him a six-match World Rugby ban. Steve Borthwick and Fabien Galthié, among countless others, had made their views known.
Across social media, Boks fans had been in overdrive for days, busily defending their oppressed supreme leader and double World Cup-winning coach. With kick-off in Dublin looming, in this new and strange corner of the internet, an Erasmus-powered echo chamber had been created.
"Rassie," wrote Griffort on the message board, "do you feel there is a vendetta against you from refs and rugby unions around the world, because you are such a successful coach?"
"Free Rassie," wrote another. "Rassie for president," added someone else. George from Gqeberha wrote: "I support Rassie 100% for being outspoken and honest ... Rassie is Rassie. Please don't change."
Rassie is Rassie. Indubitably true: "They are all out to get me." His Trumpian post-truth strategy had worked again. "Behind you 100,000%," wrote Nonnie. "They are messing with the wrong coach, team and fan."
Excitement was mounting for the big online reveal, and even ITV were hyping it up. "Rassie Erasmus is having his very own online watchalong," said the anchorman Mark Pougatch. "That won't be dull."
Won't it? Erasmus, sporting a Boks cap and black tracksuit top, appeared about 10 minutes before kick-off. "I'll probably have my sound mostly off," he said. "At half-time, if I'm calm enough, we're going to have a little chat. And obviously afterwards. It's always easier to chat when you're winning." As we would discover.
There was no play-by-play analysis. No rolling tactical masterclass. There was, in fact, under four minutes of talk during the entire 2hr 12min stream. Just a static camera, pointing at a fiftysomething coach, sitting in a hotel conference room in the Dublin suburb of Stillorgan.
It takes a special ego to respond to a disciplinary ban by building a website, featuring a bizarre AI-generated country song about "hard yards", for the purpose of inviting supporters to "watch along".
But for that online content to in effect include ... no content? That's another level of self-regard. Erasmus did occasionally rotate his baseball cap, pour a drink, or slam his fist on the table. He's always been an innovator. This was the latest perplexing creation in the Rassie-verse.
And there was no shortage of interest. Around 10 minutes after kick-off there were 88,717 viewers. But some were growing restless. "Thought we were going to watch with Rassie commentating," wrote one on YouTube. "This is disappointing."
"Rassie my bru," wrote another, "We got no sound." Had Erasmus found a way to alienate his public, this week of all weeks? @ncjhood's pithy comment summed up the mood: "Great coach, terrible streamer."
Tacitly acknowledging it was all becoming a bitter disappointment for many, Erasmus's backroom team took action. A caption appeared, top left, reading: "SOUND WILL REMAIN OFF UNTIL RASSIE WANTS TO SPEAK."
There were some interesting elements, aside from these unintentionally comedic ones. His burning passion for the game, and for the Boks, was clear. Facing a sensational Ireland performance, Erasmus looked disgusted when his fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu misjudged a kick. He looked incandescent when Andy Farrell's industrious side turned the ball over later in the half.
And this being Rassie, there was intrigue. He frequently covered his mouth to talk pointedly and at length to someone, somewhere. As a tense second half continued, he increasingly ducked down behind his laptop screen to conduct conversations beyond the camera's view.
Who was he talking to? And why? On social media people were beginning to wonder. "Car insurance renewal," speculated Monk, on X. "He's catching up on admin." (World Rugby's ban states Erasmus is not permitted "any match-day involvement including coaching, direct or indirect contact with team management or players".)
Erasmus said he would talk afterwards. It wasn't to be. The fans could wait, apparently, because South Africa lost. After angrily hammering his fists down three times as defeat was confirmed - sending his brandy and Coke splashing across the table - he packed his laptop away and the stream ended. As he said, it's easier to chat when you're winning.
Earlier, on ITV, Pougatch and Habana discussed it all with David Flatman. "He boiled over," Habana said, sympathetically, of last Monday's media conference that led to Erasmus's ban, adding: "I think we all really understood where he was coming from." That was debatable, to put it mildly, and the final word was left to Flatman.
"He knows what he's doing," said the former England prop. "It's the third time. He knows he's lighting fires under people. He knows these people [match officials] are going to get slaughtered online ... it's led to death threats against people's families. It's impacted people's lives and careers.
"I find it almost cultish that every South African I speak to defends him blindly. It doesn't matter if the point he was making was correct ... stop impacting people's lives with your behaviour."
In one of the day's stranger moments, Erasmus had earlier stood, alone, for the South African anthem. How long will it be before he gets his own one?
